claims.claim: Guy Stewart reports Wolfe's rule that a character is characterised by being shown thinking, speaking and acting in a characteristic way rather than described.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe's writing advice, relayed by Guy Stewart, 2022
claims.quote: showing the character thinking, speaking and acting in a characteristic way

claims.claim: Critic Peter Wright says ambiguity in The Fifth Head of Cerberus is an organising principle of the book's form, not only a theme.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Confounding the Skin and the Mask', Ultan's Library, 2002
claims.quote: it is also an organising principle of form

claims.claim: Wright says the existence of the puzzle in The Fifth Head of Cerberus matters more than its solution.
claims.source: Peter Wright, 'Confounding the Skin and the Mask', Ultan's Library, 2002
claims.quote: the existence of the puzzle is more significant that its solution

claims.claim: Scott Wowra reports that readers in the early 1980s accused Wolfe of fabricating unusual words, and says this is untrue.
claims.source: Scott Wowra, 'The Lupine Scholar', Ultan's Library, 2009
claims.quote: readers accused Mr. Wolfe of deliberately fabricating unusual words

claims.claim: Wowra says Wolfe's real rare words show how odd genuine language can sound without any invented vocabulary.
claims.source: Scott Wowra, 'The Lupine Scholar', Ultan's Library, 2009
claims.quote: they remind us just how odd language can sound

claims.claim: Wowra gives omophagist and cherkaji as examples of the seemingly counterfeit but real words in The Book of the New Sun.
claims.source: Scott Wowra, 'The Lupine Scholar', Ultan's Library, 2009
claims.quote: omophagist (an eater of raw flesh) and cherkaji

claims.claim: Michael Andre-Driussi revises his estimate of the span from Ymar to Severian, giving a range between one thousand and thirty-thousand years.
claims.quote: the range is actually between one thousand and thirty-thousand years

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi derived his earlier thousand-year figure for the Autarchy from a single character's offhand remark rather than any stated chronology.
claims.quote: This statement strongly implied to me that the autarchs had reigned

claims.claim: To narrow the chronology Andre-Driussi searched the text for the time words chiliads, thousand years, ages, aeons and eons.
claims.quote: a brute force method of searching for the terms

claims.claim: Wolfe, quoted from a letter by novelist C. S. E. Cooney, advised always telling a story as cleanly and as clearly as possible.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, in letters and conversation, quoted by C. S. E. Cooney, Ultan's Library, 2016
claims.quote: Always tell a story as cleanly and as clearly as possible.

claims.claim: Wolfe's critique of Cooney's draft named her habit of interrupting dialogue with long infodumps, which he called lumps of prose like uncooked dumplings.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, letter to C. S. E. Cooney, quoted in Ultan's Library, 2016
claims.quote: lumps of prose like uncooked dumplings

claims.claim: Cooney reports that when she proposed cutting the sing-song rhythm and internal rhyme from one story, Wolfe urged her not to.
claims.source: C. S. E. Cooney, 'An Homage to my Honorary Grandfather', Ultan's Library, 2016
claims.quote: he urged me not to take my knife to it

claims.claim: Keeley reads the opening line of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as a riff on the opening of Proust's Swann's Way.
Keeley says the grammar of that opening sentence carries a slight clue to the story.
claims.quote: a slight clue to the story in the sentence’s grammar

claims.claim: Keeley says the reader eventually learns why the comma is missing from the phrase “my brother David”.
claims.quote: We eventually do learn why that comma is missing.
